### D103 - A camp is not built where a drop site already serves the resource

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

Content names the roles that get the rule (`[build] spaced_roles`) and the spacing (`[build] drop_site_spacing = 5`); the
predicate asks the *worker's own* variant which buildings accept its load, so the dat's `drop_sites` edge is the only source
of "drop site". The number and the range are the reference implementation's (OpenAoK, MIT): `kCovered = 5` and
`sn-camp-max-distance = 25`.

**One deliberate difference**: OpenAoK's camp rule passes `town = false`, so its camps ignore the town centre's coverage. The
owner asked for the town centre to count, and a camp beside a town centre that already takes wood buys nothing, so our camp
rule passes `true` and a mill passes `false` (a mill must be able to stand at the berries beside the town centre).

Not yet enforced: the 25-tile range (a far uncovered forest still wins over a near covered one), which needs a decision
about which of those two is better rather than a number.


### D106 - The farm ring is content's, and reachability is asked last

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

`[build] farm` names the plot and `[build] farm_spacing` is how many farm widths sit between the town centre and the mill. The
ring's reach is `spacing x farm width + 1`, the width taken from the dat's own footprint. A farm fills the ring; a drop site
may stand in its outer half (the mill *is* the ring's outer edge); everything else stands outside it. A pack with no `[build]
farm` has no ring and every building is free, which is the behaviour that came before.

**The rule that came out of the performance bug: a reachability test is asked last, and of the fewest candidates.** Three
places were doing a path search per candidate - the camp rule (840 ms a firing), the farm search (256 candidates) and
`nearest_like` (**1,336 path searches in one tick**) - and each looked innocent on its own. Geometry (`is_free_ground`,
`site_fits`, a distance sort) is cheap and can be asked of everything; the walk is a search and belongs on the handful of
sites that survived. Measured: 104 s -> 11.9 s, with a byte-identical acceptance hash.


### D116 - A sheep stands still: herding is dropped (supersedes D70's movement)

*Date:* 2026-11-04

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

The owner, on reading that the gather approach loses its route when a node moves:

> "Is it about sheep being herded by shepherd? If yes, I'd like to drop this feature. Sheep are more likely to be found by
> scout and player and AI are more likely to direct sheep to the drop site themselves."

So a gathered herdable is **worked where it stands**. Moving livestock is an ordinary order its owner gives - the player or
the AI - and the animal does not steer itself anywhere.

**Removed:** the `herds` pass's drop-site lookup, `walk_towards(animal, drop_pos)`, and the `paths.remove(&villager)` that
dropped the shepherd's route each tick so it stepped at a moving target. **Kept:** everything about a herdable that is not
movement - ownership by sight (D70 item 5), the one-blow kill, the shepherd's-knife task name, and the
slaughter → body → resume-gather chain.

**The strike trigger moved from the drop site to the animal.** It used to fire when the animal *arrived* at the nearest drop
site; it now fires when the villager is within reach of it. A strict `distance^2 <= reach^2` never fires, because a body
walking at another comes to rest a step short of the standoff - measured **10,399** against **10,000**. The rule is reach
**plus one tick's step**, or the animal's own tile: the same "a radius, not an equality" rule the engine uses everywhere
else for arrival (C2).

**Tests:** `a_sheep_stops_at_the_drop_site` is retired with its rule (an animal arriving at a building no longer happens);
`a_gathered_sheep_stands_still` and `a_sheep_walks_where_its_owner_points` replace it; `the_villager_follows_the_sheep`
survives re-worded, its tolerance tightened 6 tiles -> 2 because there is no longer a moving target to trail. One fixture
was wrong in its own right: `a_live_animal_is_a_gather_source` put the sheep at `centre + 1`, the town centre's **solid
core**, and had only been passing because a body's centre could stand on the core's corner.

**Consequence for M3:** the automatic moving-target gather is gone, so the blind-walk hazard
(`next_waypoint(id).unwrap_or(target)`) is no longer in M3c's way. It remains real for a player who walks a sheep away
mid-gather, and is recorded in `docs/next-step.md` rather than fixed.

Acceptance: **unchanged**, hash `82efabd6f614c798` - that scenario gathers no herdable, which is the honest reading of a
change the benchmark cannot see. **662 passed / 0 failed / 19 ignored.** Review:
`docs/reviews/2026-11-04-a-sheep-stands-still.md`.


### D122 - A farm takes one farmer, and an empty one leaves a husk that goes

*Date:* 2026-11-04

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

*2026-11-04. The owner: "Only 1 farmer per farm (can be constructed by multiple, but only 1 can farm once construction is
finished). Once farm expires, it decays and can/needs to be replanted. It will cost 60 wood", then: "1 A but vanishing takes
some time, husk first ... Husk is effect only and only serves the player who can left click villager, right click on the husk
and villager starts planting new farm. It obstructs nothing as if it was not there", and on the second man: "2 C if there is
no empty farm nearby, villager becomes idle."*

1. **One farmer a farm, answered rather than refused.** A gather order on a farm that already has a worker on it sends the
   villager to the **nearest free farm** of his own side - free meaning his, finished, holding food and without a worker - and
   leaves him **idle** when there is none. Nothing is refused: the order is taken and answered, which is what the owner asked
   for.
2. **An empty farm becomes a husk, and the husk has a life.** `is_expired_farm` was already the reading (finished, no food);
   what is new is that a husk is now **tracked and removed** after `[farm.depletion] husk_seconds` (30, content's number). The
   clock lives in `World::husks` and is in the state hash: when a husk leaves decides what the match looks like, so two runs
   that disagree are two matches.
3. **A husk obstructs nothing and holds nothing.** It was already outside the overlap rule and walkable; the test walks a
   villager over it to prove it, rather than trusting the code path.
4. **A husk is a plot.** A villager right-clicked onto a spent farm of his own side gets a **Build order for the farm the husk
   was** (`EntityView::is_husk` tells the view, and the build order pays the pack's 60 wood). An enemy's husk is not yours to
   replant.
5. **The farm's price was already right.** The pack's `FARM` (50) costs `[[1, 60]]` - 60 wood - and the earlier suspicion that
   it cost 50 food came from reading unit 259, which is the *farmer villager variant*, not the building. Checked, cleared, and
   recorded here so the next session does not re-suspect it.


### D129 - The chop is a rate per second, and its remainder is carried

*Date:* 2026-11-05

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

*2026-11-05. Found by the second external review; the review filed it as a performance complaint and did not notice the arithmetic.*

1. **`fell_hp_per_second` is divided by the tick rate, never multiplied by it.** The pack says 1.5 hit points a second; the
   tick turned that into **30 a tick at 20 Hz**, so every tree fell to its first blow - 0.05 s against an intended 13.3 s.
   The felling mechanic had never run in a match.
2. **The rate is converted once, at load**, into `Gather::fell_milli_per_second` (thousandths). The tick adds it to a
   per-node carry and takes a whole point every `1_000 * hz` of it, so "1.5 a second" is exact at any tick rate and no float
   enters the simulation (D9).
3. **The carry is state and is hashed.** It decides which tick the next point comes off; two runs that disagree about it
   fall the same tree on different ticks.
4. **The rate is content.** `fell_hp_per_second = 0` still turns felling off; the loader refuses a negative or absurd rate
   rather than propagating it.
5. **A rate needs a test that states it.** "The tree is down by 15 s" was true before the fix, for the wrong reason - the
   pair of tests (standing at 10 s, down by 15 s) is what makes the rate observable.


### D138 - One picker, and it asks nothing: the script's gather action follows `nodes_of_slot`

*Date:* 2026-11-06

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

*2026-11-06. The owner, on the reachability question: **"B"** - no reachability test in the picker; the order's own plan
is the check, and a failure is remembered.*

1. **There were two pickers.** `World::nodes_of_slot` (the economy pass's) already had the rule that was measured in
   2026-10-29: distance order, **no reachability test** - `can_reach` is a full path search, and asking it of six nodes once
   a second per player cost **37x the rest of the run** (400 game-seconds: 319 ms -> 11.9 s) - with failures remembered in
   `share_failed` and retried after `share_retry_ticks` (600 ticks, 30 s). The **script's** `nearest_resource` kept its own
   copy that did the expensive thing: a `can_reach` per node of the resource, on **every** call.
2. **And it asked the wrong question.** It tested `can_reach(node.position)`, and a tree's own tile is blocked ground, so
   the answer was structurally pessimistic - `world/gather.rs` carries the note from the first version, which sent every
   lumberjack to Idle that way.
3. **So the script now asks the engine**: `nearest_resource` is `world.nodes_of_slot(here, slot, nth + 1)` and takes the
   nth. One picker, one rule, and the expensive-but-wrong test is gone rather than duplicated. The acceptance map has
   **90** wood nodes, so a gather rule used to cost up to 90 searches per firing and now spends none.
4. **`start_gather` and `validate` are the authorities**, and they are the only places a search is spent. A refusal is
   **remembered**: `start_gather` records `share_failed` when its plan fails, and `submit_checked` records it when
   `validate` refuses a `Command::Gather` with `NoPath` - the second is the one that matters for scripts, because a
   walled-off node is refused at **order** time (`check_order` is `&self` and cannot book anything), and without that entry
   a rule took the same walled tree every cooldown: **measured, 29 refusals in 30 s**.
5. **The test** (`crates/sim/tests/gather_pick.rs`) is a walled-off near wood, a reachable far one, and a gather rule, and
   it asserts three things at once: the picker **takes the walled node** (so it is not pre-filtering), the far block is
   **worked** (so a refusal is not a dead end), and the refusals stay **bounded by the walled nodes, not by the firings**
   (so the memory works). RED, watched: *"it refused nothing, so it pre-filtered"*, then - with the picker changed and no
   bookkeeping - *"the rule was refused 29 times in 30 s for nine walled nodes"*.
6. **The acceptance match does not move**: `f328ebc8d4d34b78`, 141 entities, 188 repaths, 187 made-room, 574 refusal lines -
   identical, because `config/acceptance.toml` carries no gather rule at all, so this change is for the packs that do.


### D141 - The gather radius bound, adopted and then refused by measurement

*Date:* 2026-11-07

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

*2026-11-07. Step 2 of four from the prior-art watch: genie's gather search is a BFS bounded by `LOS + 5`, with at most 30
objects reach-tested. Adopted as proposed, implemented, measured, and **reverted** - the numbers are the reason.*

1. **What the original does**: the gather search explores **standable tiles** out to the worker's line of sight plus five,
   and reach-tests at most 30 objects. The digest called the radius "a fidelity rule and cheap".
2. **The cap is moot for us** and always was: D138 removed the reachability test from the picker, so we spend **one**
   search per attempt inside `start_gather`, not thirty. The radius is the whole of the fidelity question.
3. **Implemented**: `World::gather_reach(worker)` = `(los + 5)` tiles in raw units (a villager's `los` is **4**, so
   **9** tiles), and `nodes_of_slot` refused candidates beyond it. Test first, watched failing: *"the only wood is ~18
   tiles away and the villager sees nine: the rule must say there is no node"* - it said nothing and sent him across the
   map, which was the defect.
4. **Measured, and it breaks the match**: 36,000 ticks, seed 7.

   | | before | bound on |
   |---|---|---|
   | entities at 1,800 s | **141** | **129** |
   | players alive | **1** | **2** |
   | repaths / made-room | 188 / 187 | 83 / 164 |
   | refusal lines | 574 | **767** |
   | hash | `f328ebc8d4d34b78` | `66032535f7d24483` |
   | wall | 11.5 s | 7.4 s (fewer units, less to do) |

   The match **stops resolving**: neither side eliminates the other by 30 minutes, because the economy idles once the wood
   within nine tiles is gone.
5. **Why, and what the original actually pairs with it.** The bound is not wrong; it is the wrong half. Theirs is a BFS
   **from where the worker stands**, in a game where the AI keeps re-tasking idle villagers and where a player's click is
   itself the long-range decision. Our `nodes_of_slot` is used for **both** jobs: it is the AI's "what should this villager
   do" *and* the unit's "which node, exactly". Bounding it applies a short-range rule to a long-range decision.
6. **Reverted** (`git checkout`), so the tree is back at `f328ebc8d4d34b78`. The corrected shape - a **two-stage** search,
   the AI choosing an area and the unit choosing a node within sight of it - is queued, not guessed at.
7. **What this costs the "cheap" claim**: the digest's own sentence says "the cap is a fidelity rule *and* the performance
   bound; adopting the bound and the cap is cheap". The cap is free; the bound is not, and the only way to know was to
   measure it.


### D148 - A worker only goes where it has looked

*Date:* 2026-11-07

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

*2026-11-07. The owner: "villagers go across the map to gather berries even when they were not found before… Villagers are
supposed to look for resources which are nearby when their current supply is depleted. If nothing is found, they should be
idle."*

1. **The picker asked the world, not the player.** `nodes_of_slot` (the script's gather action and the share pass) and
   `nearest_like` (the "my node ran dry" path) both ranked **every node in the world** by distance. A berry patch in
   unexplored fog was therefore a legitimate target, which is what the owner watched.
2. **D141 was the wrong axis.** A radius (`los + 5`) was tried and reverted by measurement (141 -> 129 entities, one player
   alive). The engine already keeps a per-player fog and a **resource node never moves**, so "found" is exactly "its tile
   has been explored" - a fact the picker ignored.
3. **`World::knows(player, entity)`**: one predicate on the fog (`explored_bit`), observer (0) sees everything. Used at every
   automatic pick; `nodes_of_slot` takes the player as a parameter because the question is *whose* knowledge.
4. **Scripted steps are not exempt.** A scenario `gather` step goes through the same picker, so it too must name a node the
   player has scouted; `a_scenario_researches_a_tech_named_by_a_role` was rewritten to walk a unit over the gold first
   (player 1's gold is 9.4 tiles out, just past the starting sight) rather than given a bypass.
5. **The acceptance hash changed on purpose, from `f328ebc8d4d34b78` to `dfc835be5d880a47`**, and what moved is known
   exactly: counts identical (141 entities, 1 player, 188 repaths, 187 made-room), and a `--dump` diff shows **one line** -
   node 117 keeping 90 raw units (0.09 of a resource) that the old picker spent on an unseen node. Every earlier slice was
   proved by an unmoved hash; this one is proved by explaining the diff.
6. **"Nearby" is still unbounded.** Among *known* nodes the nearest is taken however far. The radius is the second half of
   the owner's rule and a gameplay number, so it is his: (A) none beyond knowledge, today's behaviour; (B) the worker's
   line of sight, 4 tiles; (C) `los + 5`, 9 tiles. Each is measurable with the same acceptance run, and B is the one D141
   is a warning about.


### D149 - "Nearby" is bounded by the worker's sight, and the share table measures from the base

*Date:* 2026-11-07

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

*2026-11-07. The owner chose **C - line of sight + 5** when asked how far a depleted worker should look. Measured, that
number breaks the acceptance match; the shipped constant is sight + 8.*

> **This row's "shipped" line is superseded by D150 (the same day):** the shipped constant is the owner's **5**, not 8 - 8 was
> shipped only while the share table's *anchor* was wrong. **D175** then replaces both with the dat's own `search_radius`
> (villager **4.0**) wherever the pack carries it. Three numbers are recorded across these rows - 4, 5 and 8 - and their
> precedence is stated in **D358**, because until it was written the bank read as if all three were in force at once.

1. **`World::gather_reach(worker)`** = the worker's own line of sight (whole tiles, the dat's `los`) plus a look-around,
   scaled once. `sight_of` answers in **whole tiles** - adding a raw offset to it gives a five-tile reach and looks like a
   rule that refuses everything, which is how the first version failed its own control test.
2. **The owner's +5 is the failure point, measured**: reach 9 leaves **129 entities, both players alive at 30 minutes, 83
   repaths** (from 141 / 1 / 188). A 12-tile reach keeps the match resolving. This is D141's collapse reproduced **with**
   the fog filter, which is what makes it a statement about the radius.
3. **Shipped: sight + 8 = 12 tiles.** The smallest bound measured that keeps the acceptance match resolving, and still
   local. It is not the owner's number, and the difference is stated rather than glossed.
4. **The share table is a question about the base, not about the spot a villager stands on.** With the reach applied from
   the worker, `the_share_row_follows_the_villager_count` failed - five villagers spawned at (9.4, 32.4) had no wood within
   reach and "eight on wood" never fired. The pass now anchors on the player's town centre (falling back to the worker).
   Consequence, measured: the acceptance run goes 141 -> **152 entities**, repaths 186, made-room 159, hash
   `82a5063dcca63108`.
5. **The reach applies where a worker chooses for itself**: the "my node ran dry" path (`nearest_like`) and the script's
   gather action. A *scripted* step and a *share* row are orders, and are bounded only by the fog (D148) - the reach is
   about what a worker notices, not about what a player may ask for.
6. **New acceptance baseline `82a5063dcca63108`** (141 entities -> 152, both counts measured, match resolves, one player
   alive).


### D150 - +5 was never the problem: the share table's anchor was

*Date:* 2026-11-07

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

*2026-11-07. The owner's reply to D149's measurement: "+5 doesn't work while +8 does - either (1) an issue when the villager
started to look for another resource, or (2) a map issue (forest near town centre depleted). If 1, then the villager has to
return to where it gathered last time and only then look for another tree. If 2, the villager was right to become idle."*

1. **Instrumented, not argued.** Every failed pick printed its worker, position, column and the distance to the nearest
   **known** node of that column. At +5 the acceptance run had **586 failures, all of them gold (slot 2)**, with the nearest
   known gold at 9.2-18.5 tiles. The map puts player 1's gold at (24,11)-(25,12) against a town centre at (16,16): **9.4
   tiles**, so a nine-tile reach misses the base's own gold by 0.2 tiles.
2. **Hypothesis (2) is false**: wood and berries sit 4-6 tiles from the town centre and **not one wood or food pick failed**.
   Nothing near the base was exhausted. What is true in it is the conclusion - the villager *was* right to go idle.
3. **Hypothesis (1) is false where it points, and true one step sideways.** The depletion path already chooses while the
   worker stands at the node: the owner's rule was implemented explicitly (choose at the node, carry it through the deposit in
   `pending_gather`) and the test passed **with and without** the patch, so the patch was **reverted** - unprovable code does
   not ship, and the finding is recorded instead. The faulty anchor was the **share table** (D149.4): measured from the
   villager, a worker standing away from its base found nothing, and gold was never assigned.
4. **With the anchor fixed, +5 works**: the acceptance match resolves at reach 9 - **135 entities, one player alive, 125
   repaths, 116 made-room, hash `45596da62c9e3668`**, three consecutive runs identical. The shipped constant is the owner's
   own **5**, not 8.
5. **`nodes_of_slot(worker, slot, limit, reach: Option<i64>)`**: the reach is `Some` when the **engine** chooses (a rule, a
   share row, a retask) and `None` when a **script points at a resource**. An order is not a guess about what a villager can
   notice - which is D149.5's own distinction, and applying the reach to scripted steps broke two existing scenarios
   (`the_ten_minute_scenario_builds_trains_and_fights`, `the_skirmish_only_refuses_what_the_fight_has_taken`, both "player 1
   has no food node number 0 to gather").
6. **New acceptance baseline `45596da62c9e3668`** (135 entities, 125 repaths, 116 made-room).


### D215 - a farm holds the civ row's 175, and the civ's team bonus is part of that line

*Date:* 2026-11-15

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

**What it says.** The base food a plot holds is **per civ**, in the dat's resource row: `resources[36]` is **175** for every
playable civ and 0 for Gaia, and the three farm techs are kind-1 *adds* to that same line - Horse Collar +75, Heavy Plow
+125, Crop Rotation +175 - with the Chinese team bonus another `add` of 45. So the base is 175, Horse Collar makes 250, and
a Chinese farm holds 220. Content names which resource id that is (`[farm] food_resource = 36`) and the engine reads the
row; `food_per_farm` stays only as the fallback for a pack whose players have no civ.

**What was wrong, measured.** Content had authored **250** as the base - the *Horse Collar* figure, not the base - so a
dark-age farm held 250 (measured `5,000,000` raw against an expected 3,500,000) and a Horse Collar farm held **325 where the
game holds 250** (6,500,000 against 5,000,000). Worse, the Chinese team bonus was **not applied at all**: `farm_food_bonus`
walked the researched techs and never the civ's `bonus_effects`, so a Chinese plot held 250 where the published figure is
220 - measured by the new test failing on exactly that number before the fix.

**What it builds.**

- `World::farm_food_base(player)`: the civ's `resources[food_resource]`, rounded and required positive, and the content
  constant only when the player has no civ row. Reading it there deletes the duplicated game constant that had drifted.
- `farm_food_bonus(player)` now sums **two** sources with the same filter: the researched techs' resource-36 `add`s and the
  civ's team-bonus effects. A civ bonus is not researched and belongs to the same line, and skipping it was the defect the
  Chinese test found.
- The upgrade's proportional share uses the same base (`was_total = farm_food_base + food_before`), so a half-eaten plot of a
  Chinese farm takes its share of a 220 budget rather than of a constant.
- Content: `food_per_farm = 175` with the provenance written where the number lives, and the comment naming it as the
  fallback rather than the truth.

**What it costs.** No per-tick work: the civ row is read when a plot is marked out, not when one is worked. The acceptance
match does change, and that is the point - `repaths` **380 -> 552** (+45%) because a plot holds 75 less food and a villager
reseeds about 43% more often, with the match still won (`players=1`, hash `4640552242d6b45b` where it was
`42212c8e852b62be`). Wall-clock numbers from that day are not quoted: the box was at load 4.77 on 2 CPUs and two runs of one
binary differed by 25%. That reseed cost is why the reseed queue (T6) is worth more after this decision than before it.

**Basis.** A probe over all 32 civs of `empires2_x2_p1.dat`: `resources[36] == 175.0` everywhere and 0 for Gaia, `resources[84] == 3`
and `[88] == 700` agreeing with `docs/mechanics/README.md`'s U8 answer; the four resource-36 modifiers (14/+75, 13/+125,
12/+175, 402/+45) from `effects.toml`; U20 in `docs/mechanics/README.md` for the claim itself. Review:
`docs/reviews/2026-11-15-d215-farm-base.md`.


### D225 - two more debts were already paid, and the builder's queue fallback has no reachable trigger

*Date:* 2026-11-15

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

**What it says.** The two items above the reseed queue in the debt list were checked against the code, and neither is missing.
One has a real fork in it, which is why this decision stops there.

**The resource search is bounded, by the original's own number.** `T7` said "a villager whose plot ran dry walks the whole map".
`World::gather_reach` answers with the **unit's dat `search_radius`** when content carries one - the field the original itself
searches within - and falls back to **sight + 5 tiles** otherwise (`LOOK_AROUND_TILES = 5`), which is precisely the "LOS + 5"
the debt note attributed to the game as something we lacked. `nodes_of_slot` applies that bound (`reach`), and both callers pass
it: the share pass from the worker's **base** (D149) and the scenario language from the worker. What does not exist is the
note's second half - **at most 30 reach tests per search** - and that is a *guard*, not a rule: with a reach of four to seven
tiles the candidate set is a handful of nodes. Recorded as a guard, not scheduled.

**The builder's queue fallback has nowhere to fire.** The owner's rule is that a builder who finds no place looks for another
building to build - **"2 a"**, the next site in **his own queue**. Implementing it needs a state that can *be* stuck, and in this
model there is none:

- **Own bodies are not walls to their own side** (D189), so a ring of villagers cannot deny a builder a place; he stands on top
  of a friend and works.
- **A visible enemy on the footprint is refused at placement** (`SiteOccupied`, measured while writing the fixture), so that
  site never exists to be stuck at.
- **An unreachable site is refused before the wood is spent**, so "no path" is a refusal, not a stall.
- **A blind placement over an enemy is the one construction that could freeze** - allowed in fog by D58, and `site_is_clear`
  will refuse for ever once the enemy is visible, because the step-aside only moves our own units - but `settle_blind_sites`
  cancels a blind site only when it overlaps an enemy **building**, not a unit, so whether that case exists at all needs its
  own measurement before a fix is written for it.

So the fallback is **not implemented**, and the reason is not effort: a mechanism with no reachable trigger cannot be
mutation-proved, and this branch has twice refused to land code that a mutation cannot distinguish from nothing (D223's
`tile_is_wanted`, D217's comment). The queue itself already advances **on completion** (D66), which is the half that has a
trigger.

**Basis.** `crates/sim/src/lib.rs` `gather_reach` (`search_radius`, then `sight + LOOK_AROUND_TILES`), `nodes_of_slot`;
`crates/sim/src/world/shares.rs:198`; `SiteOccupied` from the withdrawn fixture; the four measurements above.
Review: `docs/reviews/2026-11-15-d225-search-and-fallback.md`.


### D226 - a farm's replacement is queued or automatic at a mill, and the setting is the player's

*Date:* 2026-11-15

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

**What it says.** A spent plot can be replaced in two ways, and both are **pressed at a mill**:

- **The queue** (HD/AoC): `Command::Reseed { building, count }` commits the farm's own dat price per entry out of the stockpile
  when it is queued, exactly as the original does. When a plot runs out, one entry is spent and the replacement rises.
- **Automatic reseeding** (a Definitive Edition feature, built here on the owner's instruction): `Command::AutoReseed { building, on }`
  costs nothing to switch, and the price is taken **on the tick the plot runs out**.

**The state is the player's, and that is the owner's correction** (2026-11-15: *"auto-reseed button and queue are shared across
mills, enabling auto-reseed on one mill enables it on every other, too. It is just global setting villagers will follow regardless
of the distance to mill"*). So `reseed: BTreeMap<player, u32>` and `auto_reseed: BTreeSet<player>` - never keyed by building. A mill
answers one question only: *may this player press it here*. The fixture presses the toggle at a mill in the far corner and reseeds a
plot next to the town centre, so the property is asserted rather than assumed.

**What it required, and one defect it exposed.**

- **A paid site.** `check_build` prices a site from the stockpile; a queued entry has already paid and the automatic case pays at the
  husk, so `check_build_paid` / `start_paid_site` run every check **except** the price. Nothing else was relaxed: availability, the
  site's ground and the walk all still apply, because a paid site that cannot be raised is a bug and not a purchase.
- **Who does it.** The replacement is handed to the nearest villager of that player free to take a build order (not garrisoned, not
  already walking to a site) - the man who was working the plot, in practice, because he is standing on it.
- **A husk was not walkable ground, though the engine's own doc said it was.** Raising the replacement was refused with
  `SiteBlocked`: the walk layer keeps a building's tiles blocked until it is *removed*, and a husk lives on for `husk_seconds`. The
  husk now releases its footprint when it is marked, which makes the doc true for movement as well as for building. Proved by
  mutation: putting the block back fails both reseed fixtures.

**What it costs.** One `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` lookup per husked plot (not per tick), two commands, and a price query that walks the
farm's cost list - all off the per-tick path. Both pieces are **in the state hash**, because a run that lost either replaces plots
the other run leaves to seed, and that is a divergence with no other symptom.

**Not done, and why.** No panel or button exists (there is no renderer): the commands are the interface, and the mill's role is what
a panel would ask. A script can drive both today; that is how the fixture proves them.

**Basis.** `crates/sim/tests/reseed.rs` (4 fixtures: queue pays 60 and replaces on the same tile; the toggle is the player's and pays
at the husk; nothing happens without either; only a finished mill accepts either), two mutations, and the owner's two rulings of
2026-11-15. Review: `docs/reviews/2026-11-15-d226-reseed.md`.

**Conformance needed**: claims the game with no source pointer — UNVERIFIED until one is named.


### D238 - "villagers still push": it is the seat shuffle, and the shuffle is load-bearing (2026-11-16, nothing landed but the reading)

*Date:* 2026-11-16

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

> **Withdrawn in part by D239 (2026-11-16).** Step 1 - "a seated body must not be past" - is withdrawn: under the game's own
> past test a stopped man *is* past and is walked through, and the original keeps bodies apart with the **seats**, not the
> collision. The measurement (the shuffle at 0.52 tiles) stands as the record.

**The report, one line after D237 shipped.** *"In the latest version villager still pushes another villager."* Nothing in the
engine writes another body's position - `push_the_standing` was deleted by D207/D208/D210 and `made_room` reads 0 - so what a
player sees is a **seated man giving up his square**: the gather place is a reservation, and it is released whenever a body comes
within reach of it, after which the man chooses another and walks there. The owner's "pushed" is that walk.

**Measured, not inferred.** A fixture (`crates/sim/tests/overlap.rs::a_passer_by_does_not_move_the_seated_gatherers`) seats three
gatherers on a node, settles them for 500 ticks, then walks a fourth man through the ring. Instrumenting `reserve_gather_place`
gives the defect in one line:

> `SEATMOVE tick=756 worker=9901 old=(421103,276154) new=(410625,276000) near=[ 11:Idle, 9900:Gather{node:11}, 9902:Gather{node:11} ]`

i.e. worker 9901 abandons a seat he was working and takes another **0.52 tiles away**, and the only bodies near it are his two
neighbours, both `Gather` on the same node and both still **walking to their own squares**. A ring member in transit is inside
the reach of every square he passes, and the seat-release test asks only "is a body within reach", not "is it staying".

**Three fixes were built and measured; each failed for a different, recorded reason.**
1. **Ignore any body that has a route** (a walker is going somewhere): the acceptance match collapsed - entities **155 → 126**,
   and `gather_motion::three_gatherers_on_one_bush_do_not_pile_up` reported villagers **0.204** tiles apart.
2. **Ignore only bodies that are not ring members** (gather/return on this node): entities **154**, `repaths` **380** (better
   than D237's 497) - and the same **0.204** overlap.
3. **Exclude seats another man already holds from a new choice, and release a seat only for a body at rest** - the honest
   version of the rule - and the same **0.204**.

**What the three failures say.** The seat churn is **load-bearing**: it is what keeps bodies apart, because the collision rules
still let a man walk through another's square in this scenario. D237 removed the crowd's *mate* exemption, but two clauses remain
that permit a body to be crossed: the **"past"** rule (D210: a collider that has not moved since the route was planned is
dropped - and a seated gatherer never moves, so he is past to every route planned after he sat) and **"a body already inside is
not an obstruction"**. Until those are answered, releasing seats on a walker is the only thing preventing the 0.204 pile - which
is the very pile the owner originally reported.

**What is left in the tree.** The fixture above, `#[ignore]`d with the reason and the three measurements, and no behaviour
change: the tree is D237's. The next slice, in order: (1) a **seated body is not "past"** - a route planned after a man stopped
must still go round him; (2) then the seat-release test can ask "is it staying" without the crowd closing up; (3) then this
fixture comes off ignore. The gate is the acceptance match at 48,000 ticks - entities at or above **155** and `repaths` near
**380** - not a test count.

**Basis.** `crates/sim/tests/overlap.rs` (the fixture and its measurement); `crates/sim/src/world/step.rs` (`owned_place`'s
staleness filter, `standoff_point`'s `taken`); `crates/sim/src/world/movement.rs` (the "past" clause and the inside rule);
`docs/archive/research/movement-in-the-binary.md`. Review: `docs/reviews/2026-11-16-d238-seat-shuffle.md`.


### D243 - the owner's four body invariants, measured: two hold, two do not (2026-11-16)

*Date:* 2026-11-16

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

**The ask, verbatim.** Four rules, each to be a test that **fails** when broken:

1. *"If villagers approach each other closer than 1 diameter -> FAIL"*
2. *"If villager gathers resource more than 1/2 diameter away from the source -> FAIL"*
3. *"If villager drops resource when further from the drop site than 1/2 diameter -> FAIL"*
4. *"If villager gathers from the resource, resource is not empty, villager is not at 100% carry capacity and changes position
   -> FAIL"*

**How they are measured** (`crates/sim/tests/invariants.rs`): one scene - four villagers on the four nearest wood nodes, each with
a gather order, the town centre as the drop site, **2,000 ticks checked on every tick**, not sampled. "Diameter" is the body's
own two radii (0.4 tiles for a villager, radius 0.2), and "half a diameter away from" is measured as the **gap between the body's
centre and the edge of the tile or footprint** it stands against, which is what touching means for a square.

| rule | result | measurement |
|---|---|---|
| 1. pair distance >= 1 diameter | **holds** | no pair closer than 0.400 over 2,000 ticks (the crowd case is `overlap::eight_villagers_...`, green since D237) |
| 2. gathering within 1/2 diameter of the node | **holds** | only a man with `progress > 0` is judged - the first draft flagged a walker 0.371 tiles out, because the approach carries the same `Gather` task |
| 3. dropping within 1/2 diameter of the drop site | **fails** | *"tick 792: villager 9001 delivered 10.00 of a load with his body 0.281 tiles from the drop building, more than the 0.200 half-diameter allowed"* |
| 4. no movement while gathering, node not empty, hands not full | **fails** | *"tick 11: villager 9000 moved 0.011 tiles while gathering from node 11, which still holds 100.0 and his hands hold 0.0 of 10"* |

**What each failure is.** (3) The delivery range is the pair's **reach** (0.4), not the body's radius, so a carrier stops a quarter
of a tile short of the wall and still hands the wood over. (4) The **seat settle** keeps nudging a man onto his square while he is
already inside the tree's reach and already taking from it - an 11-thousandth of a tile per step, but the owner's sentence has no
size in it.

**What landed.** The four fixtures, with 1 and 2 green and 3 and 4 `#[ignore]`d **carrying their measured violation in the ignore
message**, and this table in the review. `cargo test -p ruage-sim --test invariants -- --ignored` runs the two that are red, which
is how a later slice shows it fixed them rather than asserting it.

**Why both fixes are slices rather than lines.** (3) changes when every delivery in the match happens, so it moves the acceptance
hash and needs its own measurement; (4) removes a step from the settle path, and that path is what places men round a node in the
first place (D200/D202). Neither is guessed at here.

**Basis.** `crates/sim/tests/invariants.rs`; `crates/sim/src/world/gather.rs` (the delivery range), `crates/sim/src/world/step.rs`
(the settle). Review: `docs/reviews/2026-11-16-d243-invariants.md`.


### D244 - both red invariants were fixed, measured, and reverted: each fix starves the match (2026-11-16)

*Date:* 2026-11-16

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

The owner, after D243: *"I don't want those tests to be ignored. What needs to be done to make it passing?"* Both were built. Both
were measured. **Neither lands yet**, and the reason is the same in both cases: the invariant is right, the mechanism that has to
keep it is shared with the thing that keeps the economy alive.

**Rule 3 - a load leaves within half a diameter of the drop site.** Fixed the way it reads: the delivery test became
`footprint_gap(position, drop) <= body_radius` - the gap between the carrier's centre and the building's footprint rectangle,
against his own radius - replacing three loose clauses (tile adjacency by index, the **pair's reach** 0.4 against the anchor, and
`touches_footprint`'s whole tile of slack). The rule holds: the fixture goes green. The **match collapses**: entities
**155 -> 136** and `repaths` **497 -> 28**, i.e. carriers stop satisfying the test at all and nobody delivers. So the rectangular
footprint's **anchor** is the open question: `Entity::position` for a building, and `footprint_of`'s tiles, do not agree with the
wall the bodies actually stand at, and the fix is only as good as that geometry. That is the next read, and it is a read, not a
guess.

**Rule 4 - a working man does not move.** Fixed the way it reads: `settling` requires `progress == 0`, so a villager who has taken
his first bite from the tree stays put. The invariant fixture goes green - and `gather_motion::three_gatherers_on_one_bush_do_not_
pile_up` goes red, because the settle is what places men round a node in the first place (D200/D202): with it gated, three men on
one bush pile up again. So the settle is doing two jobs - **arranging** the ring and **nudging a working man** - and the fix has
to separate them rather than switch one off.

**What that leaves.** All four fixtures stand exactly as D243 landed them: two green, two `#[ignore]`d with their measured
violation in the ignore message, and both ignores now carry the *fix-that-fails* measurement as well, so the next attempt starts
from the numbers instead of the idea. The two open reads are named: the building footprint's anchor (rule 3) and the settle's two
jobs (rule 4).

**Basis.** `crates/sim/src/lib.rs` (`footprint_gap`, written and reverted this session), `crates/sim/src/world/step.rs` (the
delivery test and `settling`), `crates/sim/tests/invariants.rs`, `crates/sim/tests/gather_motion.rs`. Review:
`docs/reviews/2026-11-16-d244-invariants-green.md`.


### D245 - the original's four body rules, read; and the seat shuffle is what gates three of them (2026-11-16)

*Date:* 2026-11-16

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

Asked how the original meets the owner's four rules and for them to be implemented, each was read against evidence:

- **Rule 1 (one diameter)** - the original writes no position on contact: the move is refused and the walker re-routes
  (`MovementSystem`'s epilogue; openaok `Navigation::Move`). Ours already does this (`made_room=0`).
- **Rule 2 (half a diameter from the source)** - arrival is a distance to the object's **box** plus the job's range (openaok
  `ApproachGround`), which for a villager and a one-tile tree is `0.5 + radius` = the 0.70/0.935 stands measured from the owner's
  saves (D192/D199). Ours measures 0.200, the radius.
- **Rule 3 (half a diameter from the drop site)** - the same box test against the building. Fixed as
  `footprint_gap(...) <= radius + one step`, and the fixture passes - **not landed**, because of rule 1.
- **Rule 4 (no movement while gathering)** - the original gives a man his place once and has no move order to give him while the
  gather runs. Ours steps him every tick.

**Why rule 3 cannot land yet.** It re-times every delivery, and `gather_motion::three_gatherers_on_one_bush_do_not_pile_up` goes
red at **0.236** (bodies touch at 0.400). Two explanations were tested and one is ruled out: narrowing D210's "a collider that has
not moved is past" so a working gatherer is not past left the number **unchanged at 0.236** - not a passer-by, a **seated pair
drifting**, which is the seat shuffle D238 diagnosed. A third variant, aiming the carrier's last stretch at a sub-tile wall point,
is worse: a pair came **0.325** apart and a body ended **0.145 tiles inside** a blocked tile. All reverted; `crates/` is D243's.

**The finding, and it is the point of this decision.** D236, D238 and D245 all land on one mechanism: the ring round a node is
*maintained* by stepping men who are already working, so every attempt to stop the stepping also stops the arrangement and the ring
piles. The design that follows from the owner's four rules is: **a node hands out a place, the man keeps it until he leaves, and a
man with no place waits outside the ring and keeps 0.400 from every body.** Then rules 1, 3 and 4 stop fighting each other, and
rule 3's timing can move without a pile.

**Kept from the attempts**: the geometry - a carrier stalls **4,155 raw** from the wall against a **4,000** radius (a step is
758), so "half a diameter" is true with exactly one step of slack, in the engine and in the fixture. Review:
`docs/reviews/2026-11-16-d245-four-body-rules.md`.


### D280 - The picker asks the cheap questions first, and the expensive one of the nearest eight (2026-11-19)

*Date:* 2026-11-19

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

**What it was.** D279's port left `nearest_like` asking `node_workable` - which plans a route - of **every resource on
the map**, inside the loop that was supposed to be the cheap filter, before the sort and the `truncate(8)`. The comment
above it had claimed the opposite since D138 ("cheap first, expensive last, and only for the nearest few"); the code had
the expensive question first and the cheap one never.

**Measured, on the acceptance fixture, after the port.** `760,946` route plans by tick 14,400, **157 a tick**, and
`198.6 s` of `225.9 s` spent inside them: `114` path questions per pick and **13 ms** of a tick, while the match's own
new work was under 30 s. The fixture was **322 s** against `main`'s **26.6 s**. The pick happens about ten times a
second because a scenario rule re-orders four villagers at an exhausted tile, which is what turned a per-map cost into a
per-tick one.

**The rule.**

1. **Cheap first, and provably cheap**: kind, scouted, reach and "nobody else has it" - four comparisons and one distance.
2. **Then the sort and `truncate(8)`**, so nothing expensive is asked of a node that cannot be among the eight.
3. **Then the expensive question, of those eight only**: a node is worked **on** its own tile (a carcass, a sheep) or
   **beside** it (a tree, a mine, a farm). "Beside" is a free tile that a route reaches: `work_position` for the place,
   `can_reach` for the route. "On" is a route to the tile.
4. **`can_reach` is never asked about a blocked tile.** The closest-tile planner answers almost any blocked goal with a
   whole-map search and a cheerful yes, which is why the old arm could never refuse a candidate and why it cost a map.

**What it costs, in behaviour.** The eight are now the nearest same-kind nodes the player has **scouted** and nobody else
has claimed - not the nearest eight that happen to have a free tile. A wood inside a wall can therefore occupy one of the
eight and be passed over, where before it was filtered out before the truncation; the answer is the same until a worker
has eight unhidden nodes nearer than his next real one, which the acceptance fixture does not reach and no scene in the
suite does either.

**Basis.** The measurement above (`nine_times_the_wood_does_not_cost_nine_times_the_pick`: **66 routes to name one tree on
a map of 66**, **6 on a map of 6**; after the rule, **2 and 2**), the phase probe over `World::step`, and `nearest_like`'s
own D138 comment.

**Commits us to.** A pick that costs one place and one route per candidate among eight, whatever the map holds - and no
future filter of the map may reintroduce a path question before the sort.


### D311 - The two reseed reds fail at the same place: the plot is paid for and never raised

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

**Crosscheck (item 3, first pair).** Both `reseed` fixtures fail on the **same assertion**, and it is not the one their names suggest:

```
a_queued_reseed_pays_the_farms_price_and_replaces_the_spent_plot   line 169
auto_reseed_is_a_player_setting_and_pays_when_the_plot_runs_out    line 235
```

Both are `assert!(replaced.is_some(), ...)` after **1,200 ticks** - i.e. **no farm is raised on the spent plot's ground**. Everything before that
passes, and it is a lot:

- the queue entry is taken and **one farm's 60 wood is committed** (`stock(1, wood) == before - 60`, `reseed_of(1).queued == 1`);
- the toggle **costs nothing** and is remembered (`reseed_of(1).auto` is true, stock unchanged);
- the two neighbouring rows pass: `only_a_finished_mill_may_queue_or_toggle` and
  `without_a_queue_or_the_toggle_nothing_is_reseeded`.

**So the trigger, the payment and the setting all work; the farm is never placed.** That narrows the fault to one of two places, and they are
distinguishable with one probe:

1. **the reseed arm is never reached** - the spent plot is not being detected (the farm's "ran out" state), so nothing tries to place; or
2. **the placement is refused** - the arm runs and `place` says no, on ground that was a farm a moment ago.

**Next probe, written down rather than guessed**: instrument the reseed arm to print on entry and on refusal, and run the fixture - the answer is
which of the two it is, in one run. That is the shape every other diagnosis in this project has taken, and it is cheaper than reading the
economy code end to end.

**What this note is not**: a fix. The two fixtures are still red, and the suite stands at **920 / 6 / 21**.


### D312 - The two reseed reds were a statue, and the reach was measured to the anchor point

*Date:* 2026-11-20

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

**Crosscheck, continuing D311's own probe.** Three prints - `start_gather` entry, the plan it produced, and the result at apply time - said
in one run what D311 could only bracket:

```
DBG plan stage: from=(19, 18) to=(20, 18) kind=Some(Building)
DBG planned: Ok((1, Some((Fixed(380000), Fixed(340000)))))
DBG apply gather EntityId(130)->EntityId(131): Err(NoPath { from: (19, 18), to: (20, 18) })
```

**D311's two candidates were both wrong.** The reseed arm was fine and the placement was never tried: the *gather order* was refused, so the
plot never ran out and nothing asked for a replacement. D311's evidence stands (the queue is paid, the toggle is remembered, the neighbours
pass); its conclusion - "the fault is in the reseed arm or in the placement" - is withdrawn, and it had pointed a whole step at the wrong file.

**Fault 1, the engine: the reach was measured to a point.** D279's test compared the route's last point with the node's position. A route's
points are tile **corners**, a node's position is wherever `Command::Spawn`, a scenario or a save put it, and a farm is 3x3 - so for a plot
anchored at the middle of a tile (20.5, 18.5) the first free ring tile (19, 17) read **1.5 tiles away on each axis**, 4.5 tile-squared against a
2-tile reach, and a villager could not be sent to a plot standing in the open three tiles away.
Fixed by `World::gap_to_footprint` (`sites.rs`): the gap from a point to the node's **footprint box**, zero on it. A resource has no unit and
so no footprint and answers as its own point - which is the one-tile node it is. **The number does not change**: 2 tiles stays, the thing it is
measured to does not (the FORM of a rule, `references/game-rule-to-engine.md`). It is still a fixed number rather than the game's box gap
against a range of zero, and that deviation stays labelled.

**Fault 2, the fixture, and it is ours: the villager could not walk.** With the order accepted, the gather arm's own log showed `step=0` and
`at_node=false` for 1,200 ticks: the `reseed` helper spawned **villagers** with `speed: Fixed::ZERO`, so the man stood 0.3 tiles short of the
plot's box, never took, never emptied it, and never gave the reseed arm anything to do. The queue, the toggle, the husk and the replacement on
the same ground were complete the whole time. The helper now resolves the man's speed from content, as `farm.rs` already did; **every assertion
is untouched** and both rows pass.

**Witness, watched failing first** (`crates/sim/tests/farm.rs::a_man_sent_to_a_plot_anchored_at_a_tiles_middle_works_it`): a plot spawned at a
tile's middle, a man three tiles away on open ground, `Gather` ordered, 400 ticks. Before: `the man walks over and takes food out of it:
1000000 -> 1000000`. After: green.

**Measured.** Suite **923 / 4 / 21** from **920 / 6 / 21**; the red-set `diff` is exactly the two `reseed` rows leaving and **no red joined**.
Acceptance match (release, seed 7, 48,000 ticks) **8.54 s** against **8.53 s / 8.81 s** on the parent `373902f`, with a **bit-identical** final
hash `3f6c802027ff40fb` (141 entities, 6031 repaths) - so the looser reach **fires zero times** there, which is the proof it is inert in that
scenario and the limit of the measurement. Clippy clean, `fmt` clean. Review: `docs/reviews/2026-11-20-d312-the-reach-is-the-ground.md`.

**Found and not fixed, each with its shape.**

1. **`submit_checked` accepts what the apply refuses.** Its dry run plans to the node's *point* (`orders.rs:57`) and never runs the reach test, so
   both orders above were answered `Ok` and dropped at `step` with the `Err` discarded. A click that is accepted and does nothing is a defect of
   its own; the fix is for the dry run to ask what the apply will ask, with its own witness (a click on a plot behind a wall refused **at the
   click**).
2. **`work_position` picks a stand by compass order, not by proximity** - its ring starts north-west and it skips the tile the man stands on,
   because `plan_path(from, from)` is `NoPath`. Measured: a man beside a plot at `(19, 18)` was sent to `(19, 17)`. `approach_footprint`, the
   builder's version, already picks the nearest; the two should agree.


### D313 - A load leaves at the wall, and nothing looser

*Date:* 2026-11-20

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

**Crosscheck: the owner's rule 3 was being broken by a clause written to work around an older defect.** The invariant
(`invariants.rs`, his words: *"If villager drops resource when further from the drop site than 1/2 diameter -> FAIL"*) was red at
**0.420 tiles**, inside the engine's `as_close_as_the_ground` clause - `gap <= radius + a quarter tile` = **0.45** - and outside the
rule. That clause dates from before **D306**: touching a wall used to be a *collision*, so a carrier whose neighbouring tile was taken
could not get to the wall and never banked (measured once at 400,000 ticks, `research::two_players_can_be_different_civilisations`,
890 of 900). Tangency is a passage now, so he walks the last stretch to `wall_point` and the rescue is dead weight.
**The number never changed - `radius + one step` stands - the number of clauses did.**

**Landed:** the clause is deleted from `Task::Return`; `at_the_wall` (`gap <= radius + one step`) is the only test.
**Witness:** the owner's own invariant, watched failing at 0.420 tiles and green after; the fixture was not touched.

**A fixture had to give, and the reviewer should know what it gave.** The suite swapped one red for another:
`overlap::a_newcomer_does_not_move_the_working_gatherers` went red, and not because a rule was broken - the man who "moved" had
**filled his load and gone home**. Its before-set was chosen by `progress > 0` and its after-check excluded only "task is not a
gather", and a man who has banked and is walking back is still `Gather` with `progress 0`. Repaired by making the exclusion the one
the selection uses, adding a **`judged > 0` guard** (the sharper exclusion could otherwise skip everybody and pass on nothing - it was
one frame from doing so), and placing the eight gatherers on the node's ring so four of eight are working by tick 1,200 instead of
one. **Proven:** the position comparison fires (that is the red above) and the fixture is no longer vacuous. **Not proven:** that it
catches a deliberate shove - a mutation that displaces a working man while leaving others at work was not constructed.

**Measured.** Acceptance match (release, seed 7, 48,000 ticks) **9.28 s / 9.54 s** against **8.53 s / 8.81 s** on `373902f`
(**+9% to +12%**), and the outcome **changed**, as it must: hash `89ff37d844cfd11f` against `3f6c802027ff40fb`,
**129 entities against 141**, **10,026 repaths against 6,031**. *(Corrected by D318: the economy is **larger**, not smaller - the stockpile at 2,400 s more than doubles, wood 813 -> 1,831 and food 395 -> 1,503, and the fewer entities are fewer *finished* foundations. The sentence that stood here was written from the entity count alone.)* **Not
measured:** the delivered totals per column on both trees, which would turn the wall-time figure into a throughput figure. No carrier
is stuck in `Return` without a route in the 48,000-tick dump. Suite **924 / 3 / 21** from **923 / 4 / 21**, no new red; clippy and
`fmt` clean. Review: `docs/reviews/2026-11-20-d313-a-load-leaves-at-the-wall.md`.


### D316 - A farmer beside a plot still walks at it: the stand was half the story

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

**Crosscheck of D312 finding 2, and the reading is the step.** Two changes were built to make a man work from where he stands:
`work_position` choosing the **nearest** free ring tile instead of walking a compass order from the north-west, and his own tile
counting as a stand (`gather_route` giving an empty route for it, because `plan_path(from, from)` is `NoPath`). The witness, written
first:

```
a_man_beside_a_plot_stays_where_he_stands_and_works_it
  the farmer walked off the tile he was standing on instead of working from it:
  was (780000, 820000), now (785660, 814340)
```

**He still walks, and the stand is not why.** With the stand answered as his own position, the gather arm's own arrival test decides he
is **not at the plot**: `at_node` is the box gap against `node_radius(node)` - a **one-tile box at the node's anchor point** - and a 3x3
plot's anchor corner is a tile away from a man standing beside the plot. So the arm falls to its else-branch and steps him at the
node's *position*, which is the same point-versus-footprint mistake D312 fixed in the reach test, one function over.

**So the farmer's wart is two changes, not one, and they need one witness each:**
1. the stand is the **nearest** ring tile, his own tile included (`work_position`);
2. a **building** node is "at" by its **footprint**, not by a one-tile box at its anchor (`at_node` in the gather arm - `gap_to_footprint`
   already computes the right answer).

**Reverted, per the half-fix rule**: the witness still failed with change 1 in, so neither change lands alone. What was measured while it
was in: `farm` 7 of 8 green and **only** the new witness red; `gather` unchanged. Suite stands at **927 / 0 / 21**; the tree is clean.

**Why this is a step and not a footnote**: it is the last piece of the "a man works from where he stands" rule the owner stated as
invariant 4 (*"If villager gathers from the resource, resource is not empty, villager is not at 100% carry capacity and changes position
-> FAIL"*) - the invariant holds today only because the settle finds a man a place *before* he starts taking, which is why the
`(19, 18) -> (19, 17)` walk in D312 was invisible to it.


### D317 - D316's inference is withdrawn: the man in that scene was a tile away, and walking was right

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

**The check that found it.** D316 concluded that "the stand was half the story" - that with the nearest-stand fix in, a farmer beside a
plot still walked because the gather arm's `at_node` box is a one-tile box at the node's anchor. Building that second change (a building
is "at" by its **footprint**: `footprint_gap <= radius + one step`, the delivery rule's own shape) and then **re-running the witness
against the un-fixed tree** showed the witness **passing on both trees**: it no longer discriminated anything.

**Why.** The scene in D312/D316 puts the man at a tile **corner** one tile west of the plot - `Spawn` anchors a point, and a corner is
the far edge of its own tile, so he stood **a whole tile** from the plot's footprint. Walking there was correct: he was not beside the
plot, he was a tile away. Placed where a man actually comes to rest - his disc **against the plot's wall** at the footprint's vertical
middle - he works it **without moving on either tree**, which means the engine already keeps the owner's invariant 4 (*"a working man
does not move"*) for a farm, and the at-node term needed no change.

**So the compass-order wart is narrower than D316 said**: `work_position`'s fixed north-west ring does choose *which* tile a man walks to,
but a man who is already in reach is not moved first, so the cost is at most a longer **initial** walk - not a lost place and not a broken
invariant. Both changes were reverted; the tree is clean and the suite stands at **927 / 0 / 21**.

**What is still true from D312**: the walk to a stand goes round the plot's corner rather than to the nearest side, and `approach_footprint`
- the builder's version - already answers "nearest to where he is". Making the two agree is a **tidiness** change with a route-length
measurement behind it, not a rule fix. Recorded as such in `docs/next-step.md`.


### D318 - D313's economy figure is corrected: the stockpile **doubles**, and the error was mine

*Date:* 2026-11-20

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

**How the error happened.** D313's row (and its review) said "the economy is **smaller** because a carrier now walks the last ~0.21 tiles on
every trip", with the entity count (141 -> 129) as the only number behind it and an arithmetic estimate standing in for a measurement. The
owed measurement - the delivered/scheduled totals per column - has now been taken, and it says the opposite.

**Measured**: the same acceptance match, release, seed 7, 48,000 ticks, `--report 600`, three trees (D312 in a worktree at `338b9f8`, D313 at
`ec9d99c`, and today's `fee9cd8`; the worktrees ran the main tree's generated `config/gamedata/`, which none of these commits changed):

```
                    600 s            1200 s           1800 s            2400 s        units / buildings
D312 (338b9f8)   w  22  f  23     w  17  f  133    w  354  f  340    w  813  f  395       36 / 16
D313 (ec9d99c)   w  17  f   8     w  90  f  227    w 1006  f 1363    w 1831  f 1503       35 / 18
today (fee9cd8)  w  17  f   8     w  90  f  227    w 1006  f 1363    w 1831  f 1503       35 / 18
```

**So the stricter bank rule more than doubles the stockpile** (wood 813 -> 1,831, food 395 -> 1,503 at 2,400 s) and the entity count fell
because **fewer foundations** are standing around (buildings 16 -> 18, units 36 -> 35 - the difference is in what a run has *finished*, not
in what it has gathered). The guess about the mechanism was wrong in direction: a carrier that banks at the wall is the one that stops
lingering 0.45 tiles out with its route spent, which is the state the old clause tolerated.

**What this corrects**: D313's row and `docs/reviews/2026-11-20-d313-a-load-leaves-at-the-wall.md` both carry the wrong claim; the review
has a correction section and this row supersedes the row's sentence. **D314 and D315 move nothing in the acceptance match** - today's tree and
`ec9d99c` print the same numbers line for line, which is the bit-identical hash seen at D314 confirmed on the economy as well.

**The lesson, for the next reviewer of my own work**: an entity count is not a throughput figure, and "smaller economy" is a claim about
*delivered* resources. `--report` prints the stockpile at each interval and costs one run; the estimate that replaced it was wrong by a factor
of two in the opposite direction.


### D353 - a drop site is the nearest wall, not the nearest anchor

*Date:* 2026-11-22

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

**Conformance**: GAME `unit_action_distance.cpp` (box-to-box distance; `func_002690E0`/`func_00269190`/`func_00269220`), plus the
owner's report 2026-11-22 *"villagers prioritise dropping wood to lumber camp even town center is closer. The whole area of town
center could be dropped at (impassable center doesn't need to be reached)"*.

A building's `position` is its **anchor tile** - the north-west corner of its footprint - so ranking drop sites by the distance
to it measures a corner. A town centre is 4x4 and its anchor is two tiles in from its own wall on every side; a lumber camp is
2x2 and one tile in. Measured in `a_nearer_wall_wins_over_a_nearer_anchor`: the town centre's wall **1 tile** from the tree
against the camp's **2**, and the camp's anchor nearer than the town centre's - the carrier walked past the town centre.

The ranking is `(wall_gap, anchor distance², id)`, where `wall_gap` is `footprint_gap`'s measurement without the lookup (D246's
own measure, so the delivery test and the choice of site agree). The owner's second clause was already true and is unchanged:
`at_the_wall` banks from any side and any corner, and the impassable middle is never reached.

**Fixture**: `a_nearer_wall_wins_over_a_nearer_anchor` (`crates/sim/tests/gather.rs`), written first and watched failing.

**Consequence, reported rather than hidden**: on the acceptance scene (48,000 ticks, seed 7) re-paths fall **37,204 -> 12,847**
and wall time **12.19 -> 10.10 s**, and the outcome changes from a **win to a draw** - the faster economy mines the **reachable** gold out,
and the next pile is **1 tile too far** to be reachable: the nearest remaining gold sits **9.6 tiles** from the town centre
(`24.5,11.5`) against a gather reach of **9** (sight 4 + the 5-tile look-around, `gather_reach`; the pack carries no
`search_radius` for unit 83, so the fallback applies). The engine is right to stand the man down (D149) - **1,011 gold is left
about nine and a half tiles out, and 1,600 more across the map** - and re-tasking a man across resource types or out of his
reach is the AI's job, not the engine's (D291).


### D354 - the rule he remembers is in the engine; the picker that breaks it is the one handing out work

*Date:* 2026-11-07

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* corrected

**Conformance**: OWNER, 2026-11-07 (D150.3), restated 2026-11-22: *"Villager should return to former pile and look for another
pile. If found, work on it. If none found, idle. Iirc I already made such decision."* He did, and **the engine implements it**:
the depletion picks and the `pending_gather` carry-over choose the next source of the same kind. What does not implement it is
the **assignment** picker, and that is where the acceptance scene's gold died.

**The scene, measured (48,000 ticks, seed 7, `--dump` at the end):** gold sits at **10** from ~1,200 s to 2,400 s with **1,011
gold** in four tiles at `(24.5,11.5)`, **9.6 tiles** from the town centre against a gather reach of **9** (sight 4 + the 5-tile
look-around; this pack carries no `search_radius` for unit 83). `rule refused: player 1 has no gold node to gather`, **220
firings**. Wood and food keep flowing, so it is gold alone: `crates/script/src/lib.rs:1431`
(`nearest_resource(world, worker, slot, 0, Some(reach))`) measures the search **from the worker**, who is standing at the drop
site. The script's other call site (`:455`) passes `None` - there the script names a resource, which is an order (D149.5).

**Fixture**: `spent_pile` (pending, outside the tree - see below).

**A fixture for the engine's own path, and why it is not in the tree.** `spent_pile.rs` (preserved at
`/opt/data/cache/scratch/age2hd-pending-fixtures/spent_pile.rs`) builds a 20x6 map: one gold tile of **1** at `(12,2)`, a patch
of **400** at `(15,2)` - three tiles from the spent pile, ten from the drop site. On the shipped code he banks **1 gold** and
stands `Idle`; with `next_source_anchor` (the node he left, falling back to his own position) at the four depletion sites it
passes. **Rejected anyway**, because the same change breaks wood on the acceptance scene: **wood freezes at 68** from 1,200 s,
wall time **10.10 -> 19.20 s**, re-paths **12,847 -> 3,607** - the signature of a pick that answers with a node `start_gather`
then refuses, asked again every tick. Not diagnosed, so not shipped (D223/D217's rule: code a mutation cannot distinguish from
nothing does not land, and code that halves a match's throughput certainly does not).

**Next.** Two items, in order: (1) why the woodcutters idle under the node anchor - instrument the pick's answer and
`start_gather`'s refusal for one woodcutter; (2) the assignment picker at `crates/script/src/lib.rs:1431`, which should fall
back to the **base** anchor when the worker's own reach finds nothing (D149's share-table anchor, D150.4's precedent).

*Live verdict:* OURS — owner ruling, normalized from the bank's nonstandard OWNER tag (C15). Schema allows GAME/OURS/UNVERIFIED only.


### D358 - The reach has three numbers in this bank, and the assignment is not the engine's guess

*Date:* 2026-11-22

*Area:* Economy
*Status:* decided

> **Corrected by the owner, 2026-11-22, in one line:** *"Villager after finishing one resource (gold, stone, bush...) returns
> back to it and then looks around."* That is D150.3/D354's rule, and it makes this row's framing wrong in one place: the
> assignment is **not** a manager looking from the base - it is the **villager's own search, anchored on the pile he finished**.
> With the pile as the anchor the reach's value stops mattering for the case that stalled (the next gold tile is **one tile** from
> the spent one, so 4, 5 and 9 all find it), and the real defect is the **anchor** (`next_source_anchor`, pending:
> `spent_pile` is green with it and wood freezes under it). The reach numbers below still disagree with each other and still need
> the precedence; they are simply not what stopped the gold.

**Conformance**: GAME - `task_info.search_radius` is the dat's own per-unit number (villager **4.0**, scout 4.0, cog 6.0, fishing ship
12.0, trebuchet 17-18, widest 21.0; 750 slots, median 6.0), which is what D175 adopted. OWNER - D149's *"line of sight + 5"* and
D150's *"the shipped constant is the owner's own 5"*.

**The collision, found by auditing the bank rather than the code.** Three rows answer "how far does a worker look for the next
source" and none supersedes another:

| row | its number | its own words |
|---|---|---|
| D149 | 8 | *"Shipped: sight + 8 = 12 tiles."* |
| D150 | 5 | *"The shipped constant is the owner's own **5**, not 8."* |
| D175 | the dat's 4 | *"the dat's `search_radius` per unit"* |

D149 and D150 are the same day and contradict each other on what shipped. The code settles it in silence: `gather_reach` answers
with the dat's `search_radius` **when the pack carries it**, and falls back to sight + **5** otherwise - and this generated pack
carries none for unit 83, so the live value is **9**.

**Why it matters, measured** (D354): the acceptance map's gold sits **9.6 tiles** from the town centre, so a worker is never
offered it - **220** refusals, gold frozen at 10 with **1,011** gold in four tiles. Two different mistakes meet in that number,
and only one of them is the engine's.

**The precedence, stated once:** the **dat's `search_radius`** is the engine's number for *its own* search (a spent node's
replacement), and a pack that does not carry it should carry it rather than fall back to a number five tiles larger; sight + 5 is a
fallback for packs generated before the field existed, not a rule.

**And the assignment is not that search.** D149.5 already draws the line - *"an order is not a guess about what a villager can
notice"* - and the script keeps it for an explicit node (`nearest_resource(..., None)`, `crates/script/src/lib.rs:455`) while a
**quota** rule passes the worker's own reach (`Some(reach)`, `:1431`). That is the third number in the collision: a *quota* is the
AI's business, and the game's AI assigns from the base, not through the villager's four-tile eyes. The stall D354 measured is that
line, not the reach's value.

**Consequence for the queue.** Fixing the reach alone does not fix the stall (9.6 > 4 either way); the quota rule must stop using
the worker's eyes, which is the item already in `docs/next-step.md`. The pack should also carry `search_radius` for unit 83 so the
engine's own search is the game's 4, not our 9 - a data job, and the *smaller* of the two changes.


## Open questions (U-register, this area)

- **U14** — resource_in codes for gathering tasks. Read from dat.unit_data.tasks (see below): 0 food, 1 wood, 2 stone, 3 gold are confirmed by the variant that carries them; 15, 16, 17 and 56 are pseudo-resources whose meanings are inferred but not proven — VMHUN uses 15, VMFOR and VMFAR use 16, VMFIS uses 17, VMMIN also lists 56.
